prompt: A fibre path is upgraded from 1 Gbit/s to 10 Gbit/s without changing its route, wavelength or assumed signal speed. What happens to one-way propagation delay?

options.text: It falls by a factor of ten
options.explanation: The bits are placed onto the link faster; each signal still travels the same route at the same speed.

options.text: It doubles because more bits are in flight
options.explanation: More bits can be in flight without changing each bit's travel time.

options.text: It stays the same under these assumptions
options.explanation: Correct. Route length and propagation speed are unchanged.

options.text: It becomes zero once the link is fast enough
options.explanation: Signals still need a finite time to travel the route.

workedExample: Propagation asks how long one signal takes to cross the route. Neither the route length nor its speed changes here. Transmission of a fixed-size packet becomes shorter, but the propagation floor remains. Real upgrades that also change a route or medium need a separate comparison.

prompt: Which of these would reduce the **propagation** delay between two sites? Use the model of solid-glass fibre at 2 × 10⁸ m/s and radio in air at 3 × 10⁸ m/s; other changes preserve path and medium. Select all that apply.

options.text: Rerouting the fibre along a shorter, straighter path
options.explanation: Correct. With signal speed unchanged, reducing distance reduces propagation time.

options.text: Replacing the fibre with a line-of-sight microwave link over the same distance
options.explanation: Correct. Radio through air travels at nearly the full speed of light, about 50% faster than light in glass, so propagation falls by about a third.

options.text: Upgrading the link from 1 Gbit/s to 10 Gbit/s
options.explanation: A faster link reduces *transmission* delay (pushing bits on) but bits still travel at the same speed. Propagation is unchanged.
Packet size affects transmission delay, not how fast each bit travels down the medium.

workedExample: Check the two things that determine travel time: route length and signal speed. A shorter path helps. Under the stated model, radio in air has a higher signal speed than ordinary glass fibre over the same distance, so it also helps propagation. A higher link rate or smaller packet changes transmission time, while preserving these propagation assumptions.
